paras: The assault on a Black soldier at Delta, Louisiana, was an attack in which an unnamed "colored soldier" riding in a sleeping car was taken out at Delta, across the Mississippi River from Vicksburg, shortly before June 1919 and, according to Southern papers, "roughly handled." The only account is a passage in a Chicago Broad Ax editorial of June 7, 1919, which said the soldier's fate was unknown. The writer offered the case as an example of what he called a "reign of terror" against Black veterans returning from France.

Two weeks earlier the Broad Ax had written that readers were shocked to learn "an innocent man has been burned" at Vicksburg, which it said had become "one of the most violent spots on the map." That editorial listed earlier incidents in the city, including the tarring and feathering of a Black physician and forcing soldiers who were officers to take off their uniforms and leave by night.

According to the June 7 editorial, the incident took place "on the day after the burning of a man, known at the time to be innocent," though it named neither that man nor where he was burned. The soldier was travelling in a sleeper "on a journey across several states" when he was taken out of the car at Delta. The editorial did not identify the soldier, the attackers, the railroad or the date. Its writer said it was not known whether the soldier's remains lay in the swamps of Madison Parish or had been carried down the Mississippi.
No report of arrests, an inquest or any official inquiry appears in the coverage, and no later word of the soldier's fate was found.

The case reached the Black press secondhand, through the Broad Ax's summary of unnamed "Southern papers." Those accounts, the Broad Ax said, treated the incident "in a spirit of levity" and ended by saying that "this presumptuous Negro" would never again "force himself where he is not wanted." The passage sat inside a long essay headed "The Unwelcomed Black Hero," printed under a picture caption praising Chicago attorney W. E. Mollison as an "editorial writer," apparently its author.

The essay opened by calling the returning Black soldier's situation "too serious to be thought of except in terms of tragedy" and argued that medals won in France stirred "murder" in Southern hearts. As remedies its writer raised "wholesale exoduses" and "industrial paralysis," suggesting that Vicksburg could be reduced "to a struggling country village," while doubting that Black workers would be welcome in Northern industrial cities. The same page carried a Berean Baptist Church resolution backing Congressman L. C. Dyer's anti-lynching bill. No other Black newspaper in the coverage mentioned the Delta incident.

accounts.label: Broad Ax editorial writer
accounts.gist: Presented the case as part of a systematic 'reign of terror' against Black veterans and said the soldier may have been killed and his body hidden in the swamps or the river.

framing.detail: Essay 'The Unwelcomed Black Hero' used the case as evidence of a 'systematic and well planned reign of terror' against returning soldiers and warned of exodus and 'industrial paralysis' as remedies.
